papers.title: Nemo: Efficient Caching with Index Pushdown for Disaggregated OLTP Databases
papers.abstract: Storage-disaggregated databases decouple compute from storage, improving elasticity but suffering from network bottlenecks. Most cloud databases use page-based B+trees and buffer pools. Under disaggregation, each index traversal incurs serial network round-trips. Page-granularity transfers and caching also amplify network traffic and lower cache efficiency. Pushing down the full index to storage and caching only hot records at compute is appealing, but an efficient design must (1) provide a holistic record cache that accelerates both point and range queries, (2) mitigate the negative search penalty of confirming non-existence via remote probes, and (3) enforce phantom protection despite the index being encapsulated by the storage service. We introduce Nemo, a holistic index-and-buffer design optimized for storage-disaggregated OLTP with index pushdown. Nemo employs a tree-structured record buffer that unifies caching and buffering and accelerates both point and range queries. It further reduces the negative search penalty by caching negative search results. Nemo provides phantom protection that requires no knowledge of the storage-side data layout and is robust against large key domains, varying data skew, and partition schemes. Experiments show that Nemo outperforms page-based B+Tree and the state-of-the-art 2-Tree by up to 11.42x and 2.97x on positive point queries, and achieves up to 4.76x speedup on negative searches over a hash-indexed record cache. For phantom protection, Nemo outperforms PCL by up to 1.55x even under a dense key domain. Moreover, Nemo maintains stable performance while PCL degrades sharply as the key domain grows large and sparse.

papers.title: A Deterministic Security Runtime for LLM Agents on MPI and Batch-Scheduled HPC Systems: Consensus-Governed, Hardware-Rooted Supervision of Every Rank
papers.abstract: Large language model agents launch simulations on high-performance computing (HPC) systems, where one sbatch or mpirun can commit thousands of node-hours and a forged result can cost lives. Of 23 surveyed systems, none supervises the running job, and none holds when the control host is compromised. We fix both. Enclawed, our deterministic security runtime for AI agents, has until now served a single user; this work makes it a distributed runtime for parallel HPC and agent swarms. The Enclaweder, our hardware root of trust, keeps a compromised host from becoming a catastrophe. A launch gate decides every launch by policy alone, refusing what it cannot parse. Once the job runs, a swarm chain grants short leases against signed heartbeats and evicts on evidence, and a supervisor around every rank pauses it when its lease lapses and kills it on tampering. Each node signs with its Enclaweder's key, so the host can forge none of it. Enclawed needs no administrator privileges and plugs into existing clusters unchanged, over Secure Shell alone. Supervision leaves the compute loop of a 16-rank LAMMPS job unchanged, on graphics processors too, and adds about 3 s of start-up. Twelve live attacks on Enclaweder-keyed ranks, colluding coordinators included, ended fail-closed. Sixteen agents on a real model attempted 24 launches that planted instructions ordered; the gate denied all 24 and allowed all 108 legitimate ones. Enclawed's core and the HPC Agent Security Benchmark are open source.

papers.title: Operating System Support for Accelerators as First-Class Compute Elements in Heterogeneous Systems
papers.abstract: Heterogeneous systems-on-chip (SoCs) increasingly rely on domain-specific hardware accelerators (HAs) to deliver performance and energy efficiency gains beyond what general-purpose processors can provide. However, operating systems (O/S), such as Linux, assume that processors are the Compute Elements (CEs) and HAs are peripheral devices rather than specialized CEs. As a result, HA execution incurs substantial software (SW) overheads that reduce the effective benefits of hardware (HW) acceleration. This work demonstrates that significant inefficiencies arise from ``O/S peripheral device taxes'' (O/S taxes), including SW stack-accelerator communication, invocation, interrupt handling, and scheduling. We built MEERKAT, a Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA)-based framework for configurable multicore systems that include HAs; it allows the user to migrate Linux O/S support from SW to HW and identify, study, and quantify the impact. Here we study four major sources of O/S tax and introduce techniques to mitigate them. These include a virtual-memory-aware (VMA) communication method that enables efficient HA access to application data, a lightweight HA invocation interface, Interrupt Policy Adaptation (IPA) for dynamic polling and interrupt selection, and an HA-aware scheduler that dynamically distributes work across Central Processing Units (CPUs) and multiple HA instances. Experimental results demonstrate up to $260\times$ faster communication and $2$--$6\times$ performance improvements in wall-clock time over conventional schedulers. Furthermore, our study reveals that overall system performance depends not only on HA speed, but also on O/S overheads, resource availability, and scheduling decisions. These findings highlight the importance of treating HAs as first-class computational resources and motivate a more accelerator-centric O/S design for future heterogeneous systems.

papers.title: Who Verifies the Verifiers? Accountable Semantic Consensus for AI-Mediated Web Information Verification
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly decide whether Web evidence supports online claims, often by voting over several assessors whose errors are presumed independent and benign. On the open Web, retrieved pages can steer the assessors that read them, and assessors from one model family fail together. We prove that even for independent assessors whose every output sequence is possible on both valid and invalid claims, any protocol that decides only from their outputs and always reaches an agreed verdict never rejects invalid claims or rejects valid ones with positive probability. We present Astral, which pins all assessors to one committed snapshot of the Web evidence. With up to f assessors faulty, Astral accepts a verdict only when 2f+1 assessors attest to it above a confidence threshold and no signed challenge stands. On five public benchmarks with two of seven assessors adversarial, Astral lowers pooled attack success to 21.5-53.1%, against 54.7-77.8% for majority voting. The cost is coverage, as without attack 16.0-61.7% of claims receive a binary verdict and the rest are disputed for audit. Our code runs at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Astral-55F1.

papers.title: ZipFusion: Fusing Lossless KV Decompression with Attention for Efficient LLM Decoding
papers.abstract: The key-value (KV) cache places growing demands on GPU memory capacity and bandwidth as large language models serve longer contexts and more concurrent requests. Its footprint limits concurrency, while repeated KV reads during attention can make decoding memory-bandwidth bound. Prior lossless KV cache compression methods reduce transfers between devices but restore the uncompressed KV cache in GPU memory before attention. They therefore leave these repeated KV reads unchanged and require additional work and memory for decompression. We present ZipFusion, which enables attention to consume the losslessly compressed KV cache directly. ZipFusion co-designs the compression format and attention kernel to reduce the bytes read from GPU memory during attention. The kernel reconstructs the original values directly in registers using simple bit operations, avoiding a separate decompression pass and easing the memory-bandwidth bound. ZipFusion also reassigns memory freed by compression across layers to store additional KV cache. Its memory manager reserves space for ongoing generation and makes the remaining capacity available to new requests. We implement ZipFusion on top of FlashInfer and integrate it with SGLang. On an NVIDIA H100, ZipFusion achieves about 1.25x speedup over FlashInfer in decode attention. With 8K context, it improves model decode throughput by up to 26.3% over uncompressed SGLang under the same GPU memory budget. At each method's largest supported batch, it also delivers up to 2.76x the throughput of the best-performing lossless KV cache compression baseline.

papers.title: Free to Look, Free to Reason: Simple LLM Harnesses Outdiagnose Hand-Crafted Root Cause Analysis Agents
papers.abstract: Root cause analysis (RCA) of microservice failures has attracted many LLM agents whose investigation is hand-crafted, through standard operating procedures, fixed stages and role agents. Each is evaluated on its own data against few baselines, so it is unknown whether this design beats letting a capable model investigate on its own. We compare three simple harnesses that prescribe none of the model's calls (one call over an evidence package, a SQL agent and the Codex coding agent) with five published LLM RCA agents and with statistical and causal methods on RCAtlas, 90 validated cases from eight public datasets, across six models and three reasoning efforts. The simple harnesses are the most accurate (PR@1 65-77% on three mid-tier models), ahead of the published agents (16-53%) and the non-LLM methods (6-39%), on every model on which both families were run. The published agents fix from a tenth to all of their model calls in the program, and a case study shows how these prescriptions skip the decisive evidence. A stronger model mainly improves reliability, a multi-turn harness mainly improves aptitude, and more reasoning effort changes accuracy by a few points at most while multiplying the time by up to seven. Among runs more accurate than the best non-LLM method, every Pareto-optimal run in cost or time uses a simple harness.

papers.title: Modeling Liquid-Cooled Data Centers in EnergyPlus
papers.abstract: As AI workloads accelerate data center transition toward high-density racks with direct-to-chip (DTC) liquid cooling, existing simulation tools remain limited in evaluating whole-building and multi-year efficiency. To bridge this gap, we develop a native EnergyPlus object, ElectricEquipment:ITE:LiquidCooled, that models DTC liquid cooling for chilled-water and warm-water architectures as plant-loop components. It couples facility-water loops, rack-side secondary loops, coolant distribution units, and chip-junction temperatures within a single solver. Validation against an independent Modelica implementation across 21 operating conditions, including two full-year runs compared at one-minute resolution, yields loop-temperature RMSE at or below 0.021 K, well within the 0.1 K acceptance threshold. Our case study demonstrates that warm-water liquid cooling reduces annual PUE from 1.43 to 1.25, eliminates on-site water use, and cuts total facility energy by 37.9% relative to an air-cooled baseline. By embedding liquid-cooling logic into EnergyPlus, our work provides whole-building, long-term energy modeling for high-density AI infrastructure within an open-source framework.

papers.title: LLMs in Cloud: A Discussion on Architecture, Orchestration, and Inference
papers.abstract: The widespread deployment of foundational Large Language Models (LLM) across cloud datacenters marks a fundamental paradigm shift from stateless deep learning toward distributed, memory-intensive generative workloads. However, serving massive foundation models under stringent Service Level Objectives (SLO) exposes critical physical and system bottlenecks. These challenges include the persistent High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) wall, operational asymmetry between compute-bound prefilling and memory-bandwidth-bound decoding, explosive Key-Value (KV) cache expansion, prohibitive serverless cold starts, and hardware reliability vulnerabilities. Existing literature reviews remain layer-siloed, decoupling low-level accelerator virtualization from cluster orchestration and runtime inference, while largely overlooking defining advancements from 2024 to 2026. To address these limitations, this study presents a comprehensive, cross-layer systematic review guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 framework. We synthesize a holistic taxonomy unifying hardware virtualization, cluster-level scheduling, and runtime inference optimizations, including iteration-level continuous batching, prefill-decoding disaggregation, and hierarchical KV cache offloading. Furthermore, we evaluate resilient cloud-native service architectures, examining scale-to-zero serverless paradigms, fault-tolerant checkpointing against silent data corruption, and hardware-enforced Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) for multi-tenant isolation. Finally, we formalize the multi-dimensional Pareto trade-offs governing throughput, latency, monetary cost, and confidentiality, outlining a forward-looking research roadmap spanning Compute Express Link (CXL) memory pooling, in-memory computing, and autonomous multi-agent control planes to guide future cloud LLM infrastructure.

papers.title: Replicate What Varies: Resource Sharing for Domain-Randomized Embodied Simulation
papers.abstract: Simulation provides a low-cost sandbox where embodied agents can attempt tasks, observe outcomes, and learn from experience. Running many diverse simulation environments concurrently can consume substantial CPU and GPU memory because independently constructed scenes duplicate resources that remain unchanged across instances. We present Patchwork, a resource-sharing system for domain-randomized simulation, built around the representation $E=T+\Delta$: a shared template contains common resources, and a patch records the mutations needed to construct a target environment. Patchwork separates randomization sampling from replay and selects reusable templates together with patches that preserve each target environment's intended configuration. Its layered runtime shares compiled model structure and immutable assets while keeping mutable parameters and simulation state private to each instance. We implement Patchwork on robosuite and MuJoCo and evaluate it on LIBERO-plus and RoboCasa365 workloads. At 32 replicas, shared-template execution reduces CPU RSS by 88-92% relative to process-per-environment execution. Controlled experiments show how sharing shifts memory growth toward template diversity and unique asset content rather than instance count, within the supported sharing boundaries.

papers.title: NovaFabric: A Black-Box Recorder for AI Agents with Sealed, Replayable, Diffable and Auditable Runs
papers.abstract: An AI agent run is no longer a function call. It is a cascade of prompts, model calls, tool invocations, file and network effects and sub-agents. When such a run misbehaves, or an auditor asks what happened, logs and traces answer poorly: they are mutable, partial and cannot be re-executed. This technical report describes NovaFabric, an open-source (Apache-2.0) black-box recorder for AI agents that turns a run into a sealed, replayable, diffable and auditable evidence capsule. The design rests on two formats only. The Run Capsule is a directory of flat files and the source of truth; every database is a rebuildable index over capsules. The Evidence Bundle is the signed export for an auditor. Everything else follows existing standards: OpenTelemetry GenAI, OpenLineage, W3C PROV, in-toto/DSSE, RFC 3161 and CycloneDX. A single-node run is the smallest case of a distributed one; the schema supports a capsule hierarchy for Slurm arrays and Kubernetes jobs, though automatic parent finalization is library-only today. The report covers the architecture and the engines behind the verb chain capture, seal, replay, diff and audit: fail-closed mocked replay; a diff gate with a stable exit-code contract; DSSE signatures that bind their intent and a capsule root that commits to file names; a capsule treated as untrusted input; signer identity-trust levels with offline TSA and CRL checking; maker-checker promotion against an operator-held trust list; and a deny-by-default authorization table for every dashboard route. It presents no new experiments; the evaluation is in arXiv:2609.12582. Every count except the private ADR tally is generated by a probe script run on the public source at the v0.107.0 tag (150 top-level commands, 84 Python subpackages, 16,721 test functions), every capability carries an explicit maturity label, and honest-limits boxes state where the system stops.

papers.title: When and Why to Use TMA: A Workload-Grounded Characterization of Tensor Memory Acceleration on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs
papers.abstract: The Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA), introduced on NVIDIA Hopper, is used pervasively in production GPU kernels yet its usage is conspicuously selective: expert kernel developers in CUTLASS, FlashAttention-3, and FlashInfer apply TMA to some tensor operands within a kernel but fall back to cp.async, direct global loads, or distributed shared memory (DSM) for others. Vendor documentation describes the API, and recent microbenchmarking work characterizes TMA throughput in isolation, but neither answers the question practitioners actually face: given a memory operand in a kernel, should it use TMA, and if so, with or without cluster multicast? We address this gap with a workload-grounded characterization study on H100. We catalog the TMA, multicast, DSM, and cp.async choices made inside FlashAttention-3 forward, isolate the discriminating features through targeted microbenchmarks (transfer-size crossover, multicast scaling), and produce rules of thumb for the load-mechanism choice on Hopper. We further compare TMA multicast against DSM as competing cluster-broadcast primitives, and isolate the FlashAttention-3 paged-key-value (KV) TMA-vs-cp.async dispatch on H100 across page size, datatype, model shape, and execution phase. Our results yield concrete, predictive guidance on when TMA pays off and when multicast helps or hurts on Hopper, and we extend the analysis to server Blackwell (SM100) via a CUTLASS GEMM study on B200 that shows the qualitative dispatch rules carry across generations while absolute crossovers shift with tensor-core and bandwidth scaling.

papers.title: Waypoint: Analytically Modeling GEMM for CPUs
papers.abstract: High-performance General Matrix Multiplication (GEMM) implementations rely on breaking down GEMM into carefully selected tiles to achieve peak performance. We present Waypoint, a new analytical model to automatically identify the optimal tile size for a given hardware and input matrix shape. Waypoint estimates the achievable performance for a given tile choice by capturing all the architectural effects including interactions with memory hierarchy, instruction-level parallelism, and multi-threading. Using the estimates as a proxy, we search through the space of possible tile sizes to identify the one that maximizes performance. Additionally, Waypoint helps hardware designers estimate realistic performance on experimental hardware optimizations. We build a new GEMM library OPAM for CPUs that uses Waypoint to automatically break down GEMM and achieve performance that matches state-of-the-art GEMM libraries and helps accelerate LLM inference on CPUs achieving $1.36 - 1.98 \times$ speedups.

papers.title: Efficient Exact Unlearning for Federated Zeroth-Order Optimization
papers.abstract: Federated zeroth-order optimization (FedZOO) reduces the memory and communication costs of collaborative training for edge intelligence by avoiding backpropagation while communicating only random seeds and scalar coefficients. However, existing methods lack efficient mechanisms for exact unlearning to fully remove the influence of training data when users request deletion. A key insight is that total variation stability of the learning algorithm creates overlap between model distributions before and after data deletion, allowing exact unlearning to reuse computation through coupling. Based on this observation, we jointly design two stable zeroth-order learning algorithms and their corresponding exact-unlearning procedures: \textsc{FedZOO-S} obtains stability through client and mini-batch subsampling, enabling \textsc{FedZOUL-S} to perform efficient unlearning by preserving earlier updates and restarting from the first affected step. \textsc{FedZOO-NS} further combines subsampling with Gaussian noise to increase overlap between update distributions; \textsc{FedZOUL-NS} exploits this overlap through rejection--reflection coupling to reuse affected updates when the coupling is accepted. We prove exact unlearning for both algorithms: the model and saved state have the same joint distribution as retraining with the corresponding learner on retained data. We further establish stability and convergence guarantees for the learning algorithms and derive upper bounds on expected unlearning cost. Experiments demonstrate effective unlearning with competitive model utility and up to $56.1\%$ less cumulative unlearning time than re-optimization. Compared with first-order baselines, our methods reduce communication overhead by up to approximately four orders of magnitude.

papers.title: One-Shot Federated Model Editing for Device Dynamics at the Edge
papers.abstract: Standard federated learning (FL) requires persistent device connectivity across multiple communication rounds, making it unsuitable for dynamic environments such as vehicular networks, where devices frequently join and leave. One-shot FL offers a promising alternative by completing training in a single communication round. However, one-shot FL suffers from model solidification and cannot readily adapt to subsequent client dynamics, including new client contributions and the withdrawal of previous contributions. We therefore consider exact model editing, which removes withdrawn contributions through unlearning or incorporates newly contributed ones through incremental learning without retraining from scratch. We identify that efficient editing fundamentally hinges on learning stability. To this end, we propose F-SOSA, the first stable one-shot FL algorithm that enables rapid and exact model editing. F-SOSA leverages sub-sampling of local models with carefully tuned rate for stable aggregation and performs curvature-aware model fusion to preserve utility. We prove that F-SOSA achieves vanishing training error and reasonably small generalization error bounds. Building on this stability, we further develop two single-round editing algorithms: F-SOSA-U for unlearning and F-SOSA-I for incremental learning. They ensure that the edited model, along with all intermediate algorithmic states, is statistically indistinguishable from retraining while incurring only an expected $O(\rho)$ fraction of its cost, where $\rho$ quantifies stability. Experiments demonstrate that our approach matches retraining performance while reducing cumulative time and communication overhead by at least 36% and 22%, respectively, under realistic urban mobility simulations.

papers.title: Context Is Not Free: Carbon-Aware LLM Routing for Multi-Turn LLM Web Services across Geo-Distributed Data Centers
papers.abstract: The sustainability of the Web has drawn growing attention, as large language model (LLM)-based web services leave a substantial carbon footprint. These services typically run in geo-distributed data centers whose grid carbon intensity varies across regions and over time, so routing each query to a cleaner region or a smaller model can reduce emissions. A conversation, however, is a stateful web session: each turn reuses the key--value (KV) cache of its history, which resides only where earlier turns were served. Serving a turn on another deployment requires recomputing this history, whose carbon cost grows with the conversation and can outweigh the saving of the move. Existing carbon-aware LLM routers treat a conversation's queries as independent and ignore this cost. We present CarbonRouter, an online framework that jointly selects the model, GPU type, and region for each query to minimize carbon emissions. CarbonRouter introduces a cache-aware carbon cost model, which charges history recomputation to every candidate deployment using cached-token counts from the serving backends, and uses a lightweight gate that keeps a session on its cached deployment when it would likely move back at the next turn and rebuild its history again. We evaluate CarbonRouter in trace-driven experiments on two real-world conversation datasets with five LLMs, three GPU types, and four regions, where it achieves the lowest carbon of all policies. CarbonRouter reduces CO$_2$ by 16.1\% on average relative to FairCarbon, a state-of-the-art carbon-aware router with the same action space, while also improving predicted answer quality and estimated latency. Moreover, the saving rises further to 23.1\% for sessions longer than 30 turns.

papers.title: Governing Enterprise AI Traffic at Scale: Design and Operation of a Policy-Driven, Multi-Vendor LLM Gateway on Envoy
papers.abstract: Large organizations consume large language models (LLMs) from several vendors at once, each with its own API dialect, credential model, streaming protocol and pricing. Integrated directly, this heterogeneity yields credential sprawl, format lock-in, unbounded spend and inconsistent governance. We present the design and production operation of the Cosmos LLM Gateway, the governed entry point for enterprise LLM traffic at PayPal. Built on Envoy, it splits work by latency profile: I/O-bound control decisions (authentication, credential brokering, policy and budget evaluation) run in an out-of-process external-processing service, while wire-format translation, token metering and prompt-cache shaping run in-proxy as a Rust WebAssembly filter, so that, by default, streamed response body chunks never wait on an out-of-process call. Models, providers and prices are largely validated data rather than code. Governance is declarative policy evaluated by Open Policy Agent and managed through a control plane with role-scoped authoring, approvals, pilots, shadow-mode rollout, usage notifications and versioned policy bundles. For use cases that require it, a data-loss-prevention layer can block, redact or pseudonymize detected sensitive content before it reaches a provider. Spend scopes are views over per-model usage counters, so a new budget applies to spend already recorded in its window without migration. As of September 2026, the gateway serves more than 12,000 developers and hundreds of business use cases, handling roughly 200 billion tokens per day across more than 100 models at 99.999% availability to business. In a benchmark of the core request path against a synthetic upstream, it adds a median of 4 ms and a p99 of 11 ms of overhead at more than 2,200 requests per second on two 4-vCPU instances. We report the architecture, policy model, evaluation and lessons learned.

papers.title: WorldPager: Zero-Stall Tiered Memory for Long-Horizon World Models on a Single Consumer GPU
papers.abstract: Interactive world models keep the KV of past chunks as retrieval memory so that revisited places stay consistent. On a single consumer machine (one RTX 4090, 32 GiB of host memory, one NVMe SSD), long sessions with such memory hit two walls. The first is capacity: the KV of Matrix-Game 2.0 exhausts host memory after 45 seconds of video in bf16 and after 2.8 minutes in int4. The second is the model's positional horizon of 4.3 minutes. We show that this memory is capacity-bound rather than bandwidth-bound and that its access set is known before compute, because the camera pose is an input. An analytical model built on these observations predicts spill points to within one chunk and classifies zero versus non-zero stalls correctly on held-out configurations. Guided by it, WorldPager stores int4 KV in a GPU/DRAM/NVMe hierarchy instead of recomputing it, prefetches each chunk's memory from the extrapolated pose, never waits on a miss, and writes back in the background; to our knowledge, it is the first to place the KV memory of an interactive world model on an NVMe tier with zero-stall prefetching. With training-free position handling, it generates 37.5 minutes of video continuously with zero stalls and constant host memory, at about 9.5 frames per second. On a sealed test set, int4 storage shows no measurable quality loss; on long-gap revisits it lowers image quality by about one MUSIQ point.

papers.title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
papers.abstract: Cross-domain sequential recommendation aims to improve next-item prediction in a target domain by leveraging user behavior from auxiliary source domains. However, real-world deployment faces two critical challenges: business constraints that isolate interaction data across domains, and user heterogeneity, where many users lack cross-domain activity. This makes existing cross-domain methods difficult to apply. In this paper, we propose a simple and practical framework for cross-domain sequential recommendations that transfers information exclusively through learned user representations, without sharing raw interaction data or item embeddings across domains. We introduce a lightweight adapter that projects the source-domain user representation into the target-domain embedding space and integrates it with the target interaction sequence. Importantly, when source data is unavailable (i.e., the user observed only in the target domain), the model seamlessly defaults to a robust target-only sequential recommender, retaining benefits from joint training across all users. Extensive experiments were conducted under two setups; one targets benchmarking against previous baselines, while the other focuses on realistic and scalable conditions. Both sets of experiments demonstrate consistent performance gains for shared and unshared users.

papers.title: Multi-Agentic AI for Fairness-Aware and Accelerated Multi-modal Large Model Inference in Real-world Mobile Edge Networks
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) has transformed applications in natural language processing and content creation, yet centralized inference remains hindered by high latency, limited customizability, and privacy concerns. Deploying large models (LMs) in mobile edge networks emerges as a promising solution. However, it also poses new challenges, including heterogeneous multi-modal LMs with diverse resource demands and inference speeds, varied prompt/output modalities that complicate orchestration, and resource-limited infrastructure ill-suited for concurrent LM execution. In response, we propose a Multi-Agentic AI framework for latency- and fairness-aware multi-modal LM inference in mobile edge networks. Our solution includes a long-term Global Planning Agent, a short-term Prompt Scheduling Agent, and multiple on-node LM Deployment Agents, all powered by foundation language models. These agents cooperatively optimize prompt routing and LM deployment through natural language reasoning over runtime telemetry and historical experience. To evaluate its performance, we further develop a city-wide testbed that supports network monitoring, containerized LM deployment, intra-server resource management, and inter-server communications. Experiments demonstrate that our solution reduces average end-to-end latency by 42.9% compared with a state-of-the-art online-learning baseline and by 80.6% compared with the full-activation baseline, while maintaining a mean service-type Jain's index of 0.925. Moreover, our solution adapts quickly without fine-tuning, offering a generalizable solution for optimizing GenAI services in edge environments.

papers.title: RT-HiSS: Ray Tracing Accelerated High Dimensional Vector Similarity Searches
papers.abstract: Recent GPU generations include special-purpose ray tracing (RT) cores for graphics applications. While RT cores are primarily used for rendering, recent works show they can be leveraged for general-purpose tasks, including similarity searches. However, existing approaches do not support datasets exceeding three dimensions. In this work, we propose RT-HiSS, the first exact GPU RT-core-based similarity search algorithm for high-dimensional datasets. GPU similarity search often scales poorly for large datasets with substantial search distances. To address this, RT-HiSS uses RT cores for fast index construction and searches, followed by candidate refinement on CUDA cores. We introduce a two-pass approach to estimate an upper bound on result size, enabling efficient batching under GPU memory constraints with near-perfect load balancing. Additionally, we examine shared memory tiling and compressed result masks to improve GPU resource utilization. RT-HiSS yields speedups up to 8.37$\times$ over competitive state-of-the-art GPU algorithms across six real-world datasets.

papers.title: Amplified Pruning and Path Selectors for Deterministic Radio Gossiping
papers.abstract: We study deterministic gossiping in unknown strongly connected directed radio networks with $n$ vertices, $m$ arcs, and distinct identifiers in $[N]$, where $N=n^{\mathcal O(1)}$. Messages are unrestricted and collision detection is unavailable. Our neighborhood-clearing procedure reuses an elected receiver to secure its entire closed in-neighborhood in $\mathcal O(n\log^2n\log\log n)$ rounds. Charging each distinct closed neighborhood once yields $\mathcal O(m\log^2n\log\log n)$ rounds under an explicit degree-concentration condition, for every polynomial identifier range. A complementary adaptive-pruning procedure combines quadratic contraction with completion sensitive to the number of unsecured sources. If $a\ge1$ sources remain at completion entry, permutation selectors reduce the balanced completion budget by a factor of $\log^{2/3}(a+1)$ relative to interleaved path selectors. A geometric execution attains $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(k^2+n\tau+\min\{u^2,(nu)^{2/3}\})$ for a path cover of scale $k$, weight $\tau$, and $u$ exceptions. For directed graphs with common in- and out-degree $\Delta$, the portfolio achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\min\{n\sqrt\Delta,n^2/\Delta\})$. Every graph also admits $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\min\{n^{4/3},N+(mn)^{3/5}\})$ rounds. Only $n,N$ are inputs; degrees, covers, and structural constants are used solely in the analysis. The unrestricted polynomial-identifier density extension remains open.

papers.title: Toward Open ISA Supercomputing: A Comparative Study of RISC-V, Arm, and x86 Architectures on HPC Workloads
papers.abstract: RISC-V is emerging as a candidate architecture for high-performance computing (HPC), but its competitiveness against established x86 and Arm processors remains difficult to assess because existing studies use different platforms, workloads, and methodologies, and rarely consider energy efficiency. Our work provides an evaluation of contemporary HPC RISC-V, Arm, and x86 processors using a common software stack and methodology. We characterize the Sophgo SG2044 and compare it with the NVIDIA Grace CPU Superchip and Intel Xeon Platinum 8480+ across four HPC benchmarks (STREAM, HPL, HPL-MxP, and HPCG) and four representative applications (iPIC3D, PLUTO, OpenFOAM, and llama$.$cpp). The version of HPL-MxP linked to OpenBLAS built and used for this work is made available as open-source software. The SG2044 reaches 8.02 GFLOP/s of FP64 performance and 7.8 GB/s of memory bandwidth per core, increasing to 294 GFLOP/s and 107 GB/s at 64 cores. L2-cache-aware process placement enables near-linear scaling up to 16 cores, beyond which memory-bandwidth saturation limits further gains. Across generations of RISC-V hardware, in the context of the Monte Cimone (MC) project, the SG2044-based MCv3 doubles both single-core performance and peak memory bandwidth relative to MCv2, while improving memory bandwidth, node-level FP64 performance, and energy efficiency by approximately 100x, 158x, and 10x, over MCv1. Against the Arm and x86 systems, the SG2044 shows 8-15x less absolute performance, reflecting its narrower vector resources and less advanced technology node, but delivers competitive scaling and energy efficiency on several workloads. Its most notable result is LLM decode, where 64-core execution provides the highest relative scaling and energy efficiency among the evaluated platforms while exceeding Intel in throughput. Our results show that RISC-V processors are closing the gap with the competition.

papers.title: LooseLeaf: Enabling Serverless GPUs for Computational Notebooks
papers.abstract: Computational notebooks reserve a GPU for the whole session, yet the GPU computes only while a cell executes and sits idle otherwise. Serverless execution would release the GPU between cells, but reconstructing the accumulated notebook state on a fresh worker imposes substantial cost on every GPU cell. This paper presents LooseLeaf, a serverless GPU platform for interactive notebooks. LooseLeaf derives the state and import closures of each cell, the minimal variables and packages that the cell needs. Our analysis on 5,000 real-world notebooks shows that these closures are small, and user-cell editing leaves seconds to prepare them. LooseLeaf prepares a GPU worker with these closures while the user edits the cell. After execution, the worker saves the updated state within seconds, so the GPU is reclaimable after every cell. LooseLeaf starts 95-98% of GPU cells with no visible delay, matches the interactivity of a pinned session, and provisions 32-55% fewer GPU-hours than state-of-the-art notebook platforms.

papers.title: DualPace: Decoupled Scheduling and Cooperative GPU--CPU Decoding for LLM Serving
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving relies on batching to improve inference throughput, but the key-value (KV) cache grows with sequence length and limits GPU-resident concurrency. CPU offloading can expand KV capacity using host memory, yet existing systems remain largely GPU-gated: CPU-resident requests make progress only when the GPU scheduler exposes suitable overlap opportunities. As a result, host memory and CPU compute cannot act as an independent serving resource, leading to bursty CPU-side progress and inflated tail inter-token latency (ITL) under load. We present DualPace, an LLM serving runtime that turns the host into an independently scheduled decode engine. DualPace separates scheduling authority across two engines: the GPU engine executes prefills and GPU-resident decodes, while an AMX-enabled CPU engine independently batches and advances CPU-resident decodes. The engines are decoupled in scheduling but cooperative in execution: the CPU can execute a complete decode iteration locally or selectively invoke GPU Dense Assist for dense stages, while offline profiles guide hardware-specific batching and routing. Our evaluations show that, in decode-oriented scenarios, DualPace improves serving throughput by 6.9--43.2\% over NEO, a state-of-the-art open-source CPU-offloading system, and by 11.5--90.6\% over vLLM, a widely used GPU serving system, while maintaining the same level of latency. DualPace also preserves NEO's P99 time-to-first-token (TTFT) advantage over vLLM while sustaining 7.3--50.5\% higher request rates than NEO at the same level of P99 ITL.

papers.title: Speeding up Log-Sum-Exp: Kernel Fusion at the Memory Wall, Integer Arithmetic at the Compute Wall
papers.abstract: While the Log-Sum-Exp (LSE) function is a foundational numerical primitive for stable log-domain computation in modern machine learning, its fast and efficient computation on generic platforms (\ie, CPUs and GPUs) has been underexplored, potentially creating execution bottlenecks for large workloads. On GPU, the de facto implementation torch.logsumexp dispatches a chain of nine sub-kernels per call, incurring redundant High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) traffic and launch overhead. On CPU, exp and log operations are hardware-hungry, limiting the computing efficiency. To address these bottlenecks, we propose two drop-in kernels to significantly accelerate LSE computation on both GPUs and CPUs: FuseLSE, a single-pass fused kernel that evaluates LSE's exp and log functions on the GPU's Special Function Unit (SFU); and IntLSE, which further replaces the LSE computation with approximated integer arithmetic for CPU computation. Our experiments, validated by benchmarks across workload sizes and hardware platforms, show that both kernels are ${\sim}10-11\times$ faster than PyTorch at small workloads and ${\sim}6\times$ faster on larger ones on GPUs, where the speed-up is attributed to reduced launch overhead and HBM traffic. On CPU, where no SFU is available, LSE computation dominates the cost, allowing IntLSE to gain ${\sim}3-6\times$ execution speed over FuseLSE.

papers.title: SGL: Towards a Bridging Model for Heterogeneous Hierarchical Platforms
papers.abstract: This paper introduces the Scatter-Gather parallel-programming and parallel-execution model in the form of a simple imperative Scatter-Gather Language (SGL). Its design is based on past experience with bulk-synchronous parallel (BSP) programming and BSP language design. SGL's novel features are motivated by the last decade's move towards multi-level and heterogeneous parallel architectures involving multi-core processors, graphics accelerators and hierarchical routing networks in the largest multiprocessing systems. The design of SGL is coherent with L. Valiant's Multi-BSP while offering a programming interface that is even simpler than the primitives of Bulk-Synchronous Parallel ML (BSML). SGL appears to cover a large subset of all BSP algorithms while avoiding complex message-passing programming. Like all BSP-inspired systems, it supports predictable, portable and scalable performance. Moreover, SGL's explicit data distribution will allow automatic or programmable load-balancing.

papers.title: InferScale: Kubernetes-Native Predictive Autoscaling for SLO-Aware AI Inference
papers.abstract: Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) is widely used for inference services, but reactive scaling is often too slow when pods take tens of seconds to become ready. The problem gets worse in shared clusters, where independent HPAs compete for the same resource budget and can hurt different tenants from run to run. We present InferScale, a Kubernetes-native autoscaler that combines inference-aware signals, short-horizon demand prediction, SLO-state control, fast-path spike handling, and tenant-priority headroom without replacing the default scheduler. We evaluate InferScale on Azure Kubernetes Service in two settings. On a real ResNet-50 ONNX workload with 21-second cold start, repeated ramp-burst runs improve SLO compliance from 47.8% +/- 1.5% under a stronger external-metric HPA to 65.3% +/- 9.0% under InferScale. In repeated controlled multi-tenant contention experiments, InferScale cuts Gold-tier SLO standard deviation from 16.1 to 1.2 percentage points and makes contention outcomes follow the priority policy more closely. Repeated single-service ablations show 6-8 percentage point degradation, with an exploratory priority ablation showing a 27-point drop under contention. The main takeaway is that, in startup-sensitive inference serving, the practical value of prediction lies less in precise forecasting than in moving the controller early enough to offset cold-start delay.

papers.title: Do Bio-Inspired Algorithms Save Energy in Data Centres? Separating Server Packing from Migration Search in Virtual Machine Consolidation
papers.abstract: Energy-efficient virtual machine (VM) consolidation matters as data centre electricity demand rises. Bio-inspired metaheuristics, including ant colony optimisation (ACO), particle swarm optimisation (PSO), and genetic algorithms, have reported substantial energy savings. However, these improvements are commonly evaluated against conventional allocation policies that differ in both initial VM placement and subsequent migration optimisation, making it difficult to determine the contribution of metaheuristic search. This study reproduces an existing consolidation implementation in CloudSim Plus and introduces a matched control that retains the same initial packing and empty-host deactivation mechanisms but excludes migration search. ACO, PSO, and a modified genetic algorithm (MGA) are evaluated across two fleet configurations and four workload regimes, with ten stochastic replications per condition. The matched control achieves energy savings of 0.8-81.4% relative to the spreading baseline, the amount available falling sharply as load rises, without migrations or incomplete workload execution. Across 24 comparisons, metaheuristic search increases energy consumption in 11 cases, produces identical outcomes in seven, and reduces consumption in six. Of these, ten increases and five reductions remain statistically significant after Holm correction. Five of the six apparent reductions coincide with unfinished tasks and disappear after normalisation by delivered computational work. Only ACO under light heterogeneous load retains a 3.22-percentage-point improvement (95% CI 2.96-3.47). These findings demonstrate that initial packing and host deactivation account for most of the measured energy savings in the examined implementations, highlighting the importance of matched control conditions and workload-completion measures for reliable evaluation of VM consolidation algorithms.

papers.title: MANTA: Unlocking DAG Flexibility in Asynchronous BFT
papers.abstract: DAG-based BFT protocols marked a shift in consensus design by replacing single-leader proposal paths with concurrent block proposals linked through a shared graph, where references encode consensus evidence. However, under heterogeneous wide-area networks (WANs), existing designs suffer from prolonged rounds and degraded performance due to straggler effects. The root cause is rigid round advancement: replicas move in synchronized rounds, waiting for enough references from the previous round before advancing. We propose a flexible DAG growth framework for asynchronous BFT consensus. Our key observation is that while reference quorums are necessary for safety and liveness, they need not block every round advancement. Instead, the connectivity required for commitment can be accumulated across rounds. Within the framework, we instantiate MANTA, which combines flexible DAG growth to advance by relaxing round synchronization and flexible coin to trigger leader election and finality earlier. Experiments on heterogeneous WAN deployments show that MANTA reduces latency by approximately 30%-70% in our evaluation.

papers.title: Prefix Keys and Values Matter Late: RIPE Caching for Self-Speculative Decoding in Looped Language Models
papers.abstract: A looped language model runs one block of layers $R$ times per token, so its key-value (KV) cache holds $R$ planes per recurrent layer, and self-speculative decoding (draft with a few loops, verify with all $R$) reads them all. We find that prefix keys and values matter late: at equal perturbation size, loops 25-32 are $e^{15.0}$ (Huginn-0125) and $e^{12.8}$ (Raven-Llama) times more sensitive than loops 2-9, and the planes approach the last one geometrically, at 0.88 and 0.81 per loop. Whether the deepest plane alone suffices then depends on how ripe the late planes are: on Raven, storing only it is indistinguishable from a bf16-to-fp32 change; on Huginn, 1% of positions carry 74% of its error. We turn this into RIPE, which stores the deepest plane everywhere except a window of recent positions kept at full depth. On Huginn, a 64-position window removes 89% of the tail positions at 11.9% of the full cache's memory (1024-token context), and any window at least as long as the draft block makes batched verification block-independent by construction. Nine pre-registered GPU batches back these results. Simple models of acceptance, decoding cost and memory, two of them checked on held-out measurements, account for the measured self-speculative speed-ups ($2.09\times$ with the full cache, $2.58\times$ with the deepest plane) and decompose the $2.24\times$ fixed-memory throughput gain of one shared plane.
